utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon everybody. I apologise for the delay, but I had an urgent meeting with one of the Judges of the Trial Chamber, which unfortunately went beyond the time that I had expected. So it's not a problem. We will probably finish early today in any case. So, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and Ms. Joanne Richardson, as well as our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, I'm Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. Together with us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts, and good afternoon to our learned friends from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic. Are there any preliminaries? I see none.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's bring the witness in, please and finish with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While I was having the meeting with the other Judge from Trial Chamber II, word reached me that you will be seeking protective measures for tomorrow's witness, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed. We are seeking for protective measures in the same way as her colleague priorly had been granted. That's for the witness for tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean as her colleague had been granted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well -- Your Honour, there might be a misunderstanding. Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm reading from the transcript. There could well be a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honour, I will get back to this issue before -- prior to the break if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's deal with it immediately after we finish with this witness, at the end of this witness. In anticipation of the motion I will expect from you in any case, written motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do give us some anticipation so that we'll try and economise on time as much as we can for tomorrow's sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I know, I'm sure you will. Thanks. Madam Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Headphones. Mr. Becirovic, good afternoon, we are proceeding with the cross-examination and hopefully finish with your testimony today. You are still testifying under oath and pursuant to the solemn declaration you gave when you started your testimony. And once more, if you have any problems at any time with interpretation and with receiving interpretation in any case, do draw our attention straight away. Okay. Please take a seat, and Ms. Vidovic will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll move on to my second group of questions straight away. From the month of July 1992, you were a member of the service for communications and information which was established on the 1st of July, 1992, when the War Presidency was established. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, although I learned that only in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Thank you. From then on this service acted as a part of the War Presidency. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have the usher's assistance in showing the witness a document issued by the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica. The number is 121/92 and the date is 12 November 1992. It was signed by the president of the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please take a look at the document. The date again is the 12th of November, 1992. I'm going to quote the decision because the decision is very short. "The War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica at its session held on the 9th of November, 1992, adopted the following decision on the establishment of a commission: A commission is to be established consisting of the following: Nijad Masic, chairman; Avda Hasinovic [phoen], a member, and Avdo Husic, member. The commission is duty-bound to check the work of the communications and information service from the moment of its establishment up to now and to submit a report to the War Presidency. The decision will come into effect on the date of its issue." It was signed by the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. In connection with this, Mr. Becirovic, I would like to ask you as follows: You remember, don't you, that in November 1992 this commission was established to check the work of the communications and information service and that this was done by the War Presidency. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hamed Alic submitted to the War Presidency a report on its work [as interpreted], didn't he? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be Defence Exhibit D2...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 263. One question to the witness following your question, Ms. Vidovic. Your question was as a follow-up to showing this document to the witness: "Hamed Alic submitted to the War Presidency a report on its work, didn't he? Do you remember that?" And the witness said: "Yes." Hamed Alic is not one of the members of this commission. Why would he submit a report or were you going to ask the question? I don't know. If you were going to ask the question, you ask it; if not, I'll ask it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is possible that this has been misinterpreted. My question was as following: Hamed Alic submitted a report to the commission on his work, the commission of the War Presidency, on his work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that how you understood me?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it wasn't a report on behalf of this commission? What Hamed Alic -- what Hamed Alic sent or submitted to the War Presidency was not a report of this commission that was appointed by decision of the 9th November, was it -- or did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Hamed Alic submitted a report on the work of the service to the commission that was established. And pursuant to that, the commission submitted their report on the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Becirovic, the War Presidency checked the work of the communications and information service, did it not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, has this exhibit been given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it has, Ms. Vidovic, D263.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness another document. This is D242. D242.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please take a look at the document. This is a document issued by the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica. The number is 77/92 and the date is 21 September 1992. This report was submitted to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the armed forces Main Staff and to the general public. Can you please take a look at the document. In connection with this document I'm going to ask you some questions. From Srebrenica information was sent to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the Main Staff of the armed forces, and to the general public via the service of communications and information of the municipality of Srebrenica. That is via your service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is reflected in this document, and in your testimony so far you have confirmed this on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This information was commonly sent by the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you have also told us that in Sarajevo Murat Efendic, a member of the War Presidency of Srebrenica, stayed in Sarajevo for a while. Are you -- am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Murat Efendic was the contact person between the War Presidency of Srebrenica and the Presidency and the government in Sarajevo. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. And I have already said that on several occasions during the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regular contact with Murat Efendic were maintained by the War Presidency of Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These contacts between the War Presidency of Srebrenica and Murat Efendic were carried out only technically with your help. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you were the person who just conveyed the information by the War Presidency to Murat Efendic in Sarajevo. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These were not reports issued by the Territorial Defence Staff of Srebrenica or by Naser Oric. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that either the staff or Naser Oric sent information. I know that information was sent by the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it would be absolutely wrong to say that Naser Oric had regular contacts with Murat Efendic via the radio station that you manned. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood your testimony, you yourself collected a lot of information and you sent this information to Sarajevo or to the general public. You collected this information talking to people who had arrived in Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. For the most part, it was in my contacts with the wounded and their escorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This information that was forwarded and convoyed by way of the radio station, you did not receive it from any of the commands or commanders. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. While Hamed Alic was in Srebrenica, he received that kind of information and he collected it in a certain way. And I only conveyed this information. When he left for Tuzla, I myself collected this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are not aware that Hamed Alic received this information from the commands or their commanders?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you sent some reports to Sarajevo or Tuzla that were relative to the events in certain villages and relative to some attacks. In the way you described these events, you received information about the events in Fakovici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I would sooner say that this was not reports but just information. This is how I perceived that, and I still perceive that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As for the events in Bjelovac, you received information from the wounded who had arrived from that area?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not receive this information from any military command or the so-called military command?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never received any information from any military command, because at that time I knew that the military organisation was so inadequate, so poor, that I did not even believe that they would be able to provide me with any information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As for Kravica, you also received information about Kravica from the wounded that had arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The accuracy of the information that you relayed depended largely on the reliability of the information that you received from other people, from the wounded, for example?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now let me ask you something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness a document issued by the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality. The number is 100/92 and the date is 31 October 1992. This is a report issued by the service for communications and information and sent to the Main Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the general public.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me quote the document: "The aggressor has again used the air force in the Srebrenica free territory. Today at around 10.30 an agricultural plain from the Serbian Chetnik armada took off from an improvised heliport of Bratunac and dropped its deadly cargo over the villages of Budak and Pale it also machine-gunned the defender's positions on the Budak-Pale line. Fortunately no one was killed or wounded. This was followed by a fierce artillery attack in which the industrial zone in Potocari was most affected. They fired at these positions as well as the areas of Konjevic Polje and Cerska from their strongholds in the vicinity of Bratunac and Rogac hill. The enemies devastating artillery fire was also directed at the areas of Osmace and Kragljivoda from their well-known positions on Tara mountain and the plateau of the Bajina Basta hydroelectric power plant. As well as Jezero and the occupied territory. Several civilians were wounded and this -- in this shelling, and a 5-year-old girl succumbed to her wounds. Nonetheless the defenders of Srebrenica Konjevic Polje and Cerska are firmly holding their positions." Mr. Becirovic, this is one of the reports that were sent via the service for communications and information to Sarajevo, to the Main Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, amongst others. Do you agree with me that this is indeed where it went?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the addressees is the Main Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document was received by the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina because it bears its stamp?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was sent by the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Neither the service nor you personally were duty-bound by the Territorial Defence staff to send reports to the Main Staff of the armed forces. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, if it could be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be Exhibit Number D264. One question, Witness: Your department, though I may call it like that, the communications and reporting service of Srebrenica municipality, would send this message via radio to an amateur radio -- to a ham operator or -- who would -- would he receive instructions to draw it up in writing? Would he receive it in writing or would he receive it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How would he receive it? Because he would hear the words, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. I've already said that this operator would either handwrite it or tape it by means of a tape recorder. And then, if possible, he would type it and the document would receive the form you have in front of you. In Sarajevo, Murat Efendic was duty-bound to take the information to the addressees indicated on the document. There was no other way to send information from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's take -- let me take you through the whole process. Who would come to your office with this message to be relayed to Sarajevo? Who would it be, for example, in this case who would it be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this particular case, it would be Hamed Alic. At that time, Hamed was the head of the service for communications and information. He would bring the information to me. He would bring me a piece of paper, and with ham radio operators in Sarajevo I had the so-called skads, or slots, when we would communicate. One slot was in the morning and one slot was in the afternoon. And during those slots when we talked, I would forward this information if I could because it very often happened that the information that was sent from Srebrenica was disrupted by the Serbian forces. That's why I was very often forced to send one piece of information in several piecemeals over a number of hours. I had to change frequencies in order to complete the job, in order to send the entire information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in drawing in message to be relayed, in drawing it up, this message to be relayed to Sarajevo, Hamed Alic would receive the information from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, he collected information the same way I did once he left. I don't know whether he contacted the War Presidency every time he drafted a piece of information. However, he did it more often than I did it later on, once he left, in agreement with the president of the War Presidency, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But his job was to receive information and then relay it over to Sarajevo, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So on military matters, who would give him information? Where would he get the information from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases in the same way I did when he left, in the hospital, from the wounded who had arrived, or from their escorts, those people who arrived together with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you would then relay this message in whole or in pieces, I can understand you why, to a contact, ham radio contact, that you would have, that you would establish. I take it from what you are telling me that in spite of the difficulties that there obviously were, this was pretty much well-organised in that I see here that you relayed it on the 1st of November. And on the same day, it was received by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So whoever received your radio communication, in whole or in piece, transcribed it, reduced it into writing, and handed it over to the Ministry of Defence on the same day. So do I take it that the system was pretty well-organised, or am I wrong in my assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If you think that this is good organisation, then yes, we were well-organised. However, it very often happened that the radio operator who was sitting in Sarajevo could not receive or forward information on the same day. Sometimes he would do it on the following day. However, the goal was always achieved. The goal was for the information to arrive at the addressee's address, and it eventually did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And let's take it -- in this case, the person who received the message on the other end and he had his own code or signal 4, N4SGS. He would be known at the ministry in Sarajevo, wouldn't he, because otherwise anyone could walk in with a typed message and say, I have received this from Srebrenica municipality today. So it had to be someone known and someone trusted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably. I don't know where this person worked, but it seems to me that this information was faxed through. If I am not mistaken, there is a telephone number in the upper left corner, the number of the telephone from which this information was sent to the Main Staff of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean to say, because earlier on in your testimony some days -- a few days back you told us that you were the one who managed to establish contact with some ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you selected these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. What do you mean? I established contact with anybody who -- who answered me in Sarajevo. I didn't know people in Sarajevo. I don't know who -- I didn't know who was on the other end. I did not have any alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you were going to transmit to and through that person confidential and top-secret messages for the Ministry of Defence, wouldn't you take the burden or anyone else take the burden of checking who the person was at the other end was and whether he was trustworthy or not, whether he would be trusted or not. It could be a Serb for all that matter with ham radio address in Sarajevo. You wouldn't be able to know whether he was a Serb or a Muslim. Would you trust sending him a message like this, not knowing whether he was a Serb or a Muslim and whether he would relay this to where you wanted it to get?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it could happen. However, Murat Efendic was in Sarajevo. In most cases he was the one who received this information and took it personally to the addressees; and if not personally, then he would fax it through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, was Murat Efendic informed as to who your contacts were so that he could check on them, whether they were trustworthy or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. He was sitting next to the ham radio operator while the message was being transmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the way it operated, you would inform the ham radio operator that you would be transmitting a message and he would call Murat Efendic to be present. And then you would know exactly what time you would relay the message and that would be the time when Murat Efendic will be there present next to the ham radio operator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. I've already said that we had two allocated slots. One was in the morning and the other one was in the afternoon. During those slots, Murat Efendic would go to the place where the ham radio was, irrespective of the fact whether there was something transmitted or not. And we talked about the situation in town because he had relatives over there still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that's clear enough. Judge Eser. Sorry, Madam Vidovic, we've taken over, but I think this needed to be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you for bringing these matters up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I still have some problems to understand the proceeding. Now, if you take D264, am I correct in assuming that the original of this report was produced in Sarajevo? It was written in Sarajevo? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, when you collected -- and it was on the 31st of October, at that time I think the other person was still in Srebrenica. Now, this is a rather long report. Was it given to you in writing or did Alic tell you what you should transmit by radio to Sarajevo? Was there something existing in writing which you transmitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I received all the reports in writing, whether typewritten or handwritten. These written reports would then be placed in a file in Srebrenica. That's what I would do. Maybe you noticed that I always put the date and time on all of my reports as well as the call signal of the addressee. Here you don't have anything like that because the whole thing was drawn up in Sarajevo. I may have sent it one day previously, but the day it was actually received by the operator, Murat Efendic, in Sarajevo, they then prepared this to be faxed through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And if we compare it, let's say, to Prosecution Exhibit P310 where you had your signature there. This was faxed, so do I understand it correctly that in this case you received the report already written and then you faxed it to Sarajevo? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I would radio information. Information of documents containing information on my signature were found in Srebrenica and were brought over from Srebrenica. Information such as a specific copy is something that was found in Sarajevo in the archives, but the substance is the same, except that this specific document was not in Srebrenica, one in which I entered my own information on the date and time that it was forwarded. I was in no position to fax information from Srebrenica for the simple reason that the phone lines were down at the time. As I've explained, I would read reports into a microphone, and then the Sarajevo-based operator would transcribe this information or tape it first and transcribe it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there may have been a slight misunderstanding. You would report that during the examination-in-chief you were shown some documents which at the top right corner showed some words plus your signature plus a date and on the top left corner showed a telephone number which you yourself said that that should indicate that that document was faxed. There were a number of documents that you faxed from Srebrenica to Sarajevo, weren't there, until it was possible to fax?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then after certain moment, you couldn't fax anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As long as documents were being sent by fax, you didn't have my signature or the time and date. The moment we could no longer fax things through, when we started radioing messages, that's when I started writing these things down. You couldn't find a -- another document with all this information that I've now spoken about or my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But what did you write down? Did you write down the report or only that you have done something with the report, which you received from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Information usually found on such documents as I have been shown, if I produced the documents, I wrote them like that. And I said that they were in fact information. And the fact that a report says "information," that for me was the most natural name to give this sort of report or any information, indeed, to be forwarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So it may be the case that some of the documents, exhibits, have been drafted by you and then transmitted by radio -- via radio to Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And as long as Alic still was in Srebrenica, you would take reports written by him to you and you transmitted them to Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough. Now it has cleared much of what seemed to be unclear until a few minutes ago. Sorry again to you, Madam Vidovic, but I think it was necessary. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, at any rate, this person who was receiving information over in Sarajevo could not on their own write down the sender. They would always be given accurate information on who the sender was and what the substance was of what you were sending? In other words, this person would never make things up or added things. Would I be right in saying this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony on Friday, you were shown several documents by the Prosecutor, and a minute ago you were asked about these documents by the Chamber. These documents said "municipal staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica," in the heading, communications and information service, and the subject of these documents were these reports or information on the situation in Srebrenica. It is in relation to this that I would like to ask you a number of questions. I would also like to show you some of these documents as well as some other documents. First and foremost, Mr. Becirovic, 12 years later you no longer remember the specific headings that these documents had, the documents, call them appeals or whatever else you like, that you were sending from Srebrenica to Sarajevo. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even back then in 1992 and 1993, this didn't strike me as essential. The important thing was to send information out of Srebrenica. To the extent that I can now remember, all information went through the communications and information service in the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified about things that you were asked by the OTP, and you said that you never received from the Territorial Defence Staff any sort of documents. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is your conclusion that the reports that say "staff" in the heading and that you were shown by the Prosecutor were sent by you to Sarajevo, based on the memory and what the substance was of those documents. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is also your conclusion now that you sent those documents based on what you believed, that those documents have something that resemble your signature or an abbreviated form of your signature as well as other details that you claim might have been written by you. Mr. Becirovic, would you agree with me when I say that after the fall of Srebrenica, many documents were left behind that bore your signature or samples of your handwriting or your initials. Wouldn't that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. If I may just clarify, I would like to say there was a document I was shown here and I noticed certain information in it that I was not want to write down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It's apparent that we may be going down a line of questioning regarding documents without any exhibit number or having the witness look at the particular document with any reference, so it's beginning to be a little bit ambiguous using the word document and having the witness testify about, you know, anything with respect to that document, be it his signature or information. I think it would be best for these proceedings if we begin to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're 100 per cent right, Ms. Richardson, but that's how they will be treated. If they remain ambiguous, that's how they will be treated. So coming from an adversarial system like I do, you know that I will not interfere. Thank you for your observation. At the end of the day, you have opened Ms. Vidovic's eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be using specific documents very soon. Right now I'm talking about all the documents of a military or political nature that were left behind in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, these documents that remained in Srebrenica that bore your signature, samples of your handwriting, or initials, whatever they were, you are aware that they fell into the hands of the Serb forces and the Serb intelligence services after the fall of Srebrenica. Wouldn't that be right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now to show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Vidovic and Mr. Becirovic. For example, you said "yes" before she hadn't even finished her question. Please allow an interval of time between question and answer because we need to follow, we need to have what you're saying translated to us, and we can't -- and you're also creating difficulties for the interpreters. So please allow Madam Vidovic to finish her question, allow a short interval of time, then you give your answer, and then after a short interval of time you proceed to the next question, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I have the usher's assistance. I would like to show the witness document 1081621. I would like to say that we obtained these documents at the last minute, and we were in no position to secure an English translation. But we will have these two in due course. They will be submitted to the Chamber as soon as tomorrow, therefore can we have these documents placed on the ELMO, please. I will be quoting so that the interpreters can follow what I am saying. Can the usher please show the witness document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I can't follow you. I can't follow you, Ms. Vidovic. You said, at least from what I have on the transcript here, document 1081621. Which one is that? Because the -- it's definitely not the first two pages. No, no, the second two -- the second batch is 01801622.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then 1623, and it's not 1080, it's 0180. So let's clear this up so we can follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 018, yes. Thank you, Your Honours. This is 01801621.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality. The number is 80/92, and the date is 25th of September, 1992. The subject is: Report. The document was signed by the communications and information service of Srebrenica municipality. Your Honours, and this goes to the witness, too, we have added the following number, P134 to the document, and the ERN is 01787841. This document bears the following heading: Staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica, communications and information service, 80/92, the date is 25th of September, 1992. It was signed also by the communications and informations service of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, if you could look at this carefully, both these documents carefully, and please if you could just read -- if you could please read the following document first, 01787841, which is OTP number bearing the following heading: Srebrenica municipal staff. Please, Witness, can you have a look at this document. Witness, can you now please have a look at the other document if you've finished looking at this one. Witness, can you please now look at the other document 01801621. The heading is: War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality. The number is the same, 80/92, and the date is also the same, the 25th of September, 1992. I will ask you a number of questions in relation to this. First of all, do you agree -- please look at the protocol numbers and the date. Do you agree that both these documents have the same protocol number and the same date and that they were both signed by the same service, the information -- the communications and information service of Srebrenica municipality. Would I be right in stating that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please go through the other document too. I'm putting it to you that the substance of this other document is identical to the previous one. Can you have a look, please. This is of great consequence to us. Can you please compare the two documents in terms of substance. Witness, do you agree that in terms of substance these two documents are identical?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I read halfway through the first and halfway through the second document. I haven't finished reading either. What I read appears to be entirely identical. It's the same information. It's the same events. It's the same report. But there is a difference in the heading. The sender is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm about to ask you something about that, Witness. The only difference between these two consists in the fact that one document has the War Presidency in the heading and the other document has the municipal staff -- the municipal TO -- the municipal staff of the TO in the heading. But if you could please now look at 01801621, if you could please look at the upper right corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we are -- this is getting all very much confused. Let's clear this up first of all. Let's agree that the text of the message is the same. Do you agree Defence, Prosecution, and Witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at this time we don't have the English. We're trying to see if it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but even if you look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have the English either of the first one, but if I look at the B/C/S text, I can easily see that it is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact maybe I can be of some assistance. We located P134 and this is the English and it appears to be the English of what the Defence exhibit is using at the moment, which is 01787841. And in fact, as I read the English, it is -- we can agree to the fact that there is a difference in the sender, one is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But for the time being, the text I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can agree on the text, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we agree that the sender is different? In the first one, which has 01787841, it seems to be Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the "opstina ratno predsjednistvo" which is the territorial staff of the Srebrenica municipality, while the other one is the ratno -- the War Presidency of the -- of Srebrenica. Do you agree on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree. I have, as I said, the English, and I do agree with what Your Honour has just stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you agree that the protocol number 80/92 appears to be the same on both documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree also that the date of this document seems to be or purports to be the 25th of September of 1992 in both cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's agreed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that the subject matter is report in both instances?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree that the addressees, who should have received these two messages, are different, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And let's go through those. Let's start with the first of these documents, 01787841. The first addressee is GS Sarajevo, which means, if anyone can translate to me and to others. G --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Staff, Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: [Previous translations continues]... can I be of assistance to the Bench by handing up -- excuse me -- as I said before, we have the English translation. Maybe the registrar can hand the Bench of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So while this first document purports to have this report transmitted to these three persons, GS Oruzanih Snaga in Sarajevo, the Main Staff in Sarajevo, and then OKS Oruzanih Snaga in Tuzla, the Main Staff in Tuzla. And then thirdly, publicity. The other document is meant to be transmitted to the Presidency of BiH, the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and publicity. Do you agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So now we have cleared that up. Let me clear a few other things. Do you agree that the second of these documents, the one which has the ERN number 01801621 at the top right left-hand corner shows that -- or indicates that it was faxed and that it was faxed successfully; in other words, that it -- the machine from which it was faxed showed that it had been transmitted -- that it went through, in other words. Do you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the second document -- on the first document 841, 7841, there is no indication that this document was faxed?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there is indication on the top right-hand corner that it was relayed by radio to -- at 16 hours to Ilijas, who happens to be the same guy we saw earlier, with this call signal. I don't need to repeat it. You have it there. Through Nada as well with the call signal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now your question, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, we used this document with the War Presidency in the heading, the Srebrenica War Presidency. Could you now please look at the upper right corner. Would you agree that this document bears the incoming stamp of the Bosnia and Herzegovina armed forces, and that it was received on the 26th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please turn the page and look at the lower left corner. It says "received by ham radio 4M4SGS, Sarajevo received by Ilijas Omerovic."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document also bears the stamp of the town secretariat for national defence, the OID service, and the control sector?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that Mr. Omerovic worked with the town's secretariat for national defence?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Judging by the stamp, it strikes me as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that it was from the secretariat that he faxed this stamp to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you go back to page 1, it says: "From GSNO, Sarajevo." GSNO stands for the town secretariat for national defence. Is that correct, Mr. Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, would I be right to state that this in fact was the document which made it to Sarajevo, the one bearing the War Presidency of Srebrenica in its heading? Doesn't the incoming stamp of the army appear to confirm that as well as the incoming stamp of the town's secretariat for national defence, as well as Ilijas Omerovic's signature?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because this needs some clarification. Look at the first one of these documents, the ones which have ERN number 01787841, which at the top right-hand corner shows in handwriting the time and date when it's supposed to have been transmitted. If I were to ask you: Where do you think the Prosecution recovered this document, would it be from Sarajevo or would it be from Srebrenica? What would you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's what I thought you would answer. And if you look at the second document, the one with the stamp of the army, where would you say that the Prosecution recovered this document, from Srebrenica or from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, as a matter of fact, the ham radio station that Ilijas Omerovic operated, please look at its indication at the end of the document that the Judge has just shown to you and of which you have said that it was located in Sarajevo. Can you look at the second page of the document where it says received through the ham radio station. Please look at that. The ham radio station which was manned by Ilijas Omerovic had the marking 4N4SGS, and this is reflected in this document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the second document, the one that you said that it was probably located in Srebrenica; in its heading is the armed forces staff. Please, it says here "at 1600 hours the radio station 4SGS Ilijas," and in this connection I'm going to ask you as follows. You were working in Srebrenica and you knew exactly which one was Mr. Ilija Omerovic's radio station, and you would not have made a mistake in noting the designating mark of that station. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew the name and the code of that station.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this number here in document bearing number 01787841 is wrong? It is not the sign of the station that Ilija Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Omerovic manned?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain. I don't remember whether I put the entire name or the entire sign of the ham radio station at all times. I did on most occasions. On some occasions, I didn't. So I can't be sure of that as I sit here. It is possible, though, that somebody, not knowing what the sign was, put a wrong sign on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You certainly were familiar with the signs of all the radio stations, otherwise you would not have been able to get in touch with all those radio stations. You would not have put a wrong code for any of the radio stations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, pardon me, Madam Vidovic. Now, in your country, I don't know how it operated in your country, but I suspect that it operates pretty much the same worldwide. Ham radio operator licensed, in other words, registered ham radio operator in Sarajevo, would he have a call sign which is indicative of Sarajevo, while, for example, another ham radio operator from Belgrade would have a call signal that could identify with Belgrade or a call signal that would identify with him a particular location? Would SGS, for example, mean anything to you in a call sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is no reason why someone who wouldn't know the call sign of this Ilija Omerovic would put an SGS at the end of the call signal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who are aware of the entire code -- let me explain. There is an association of ham radio stations in Bosnia and Herzegovina that operated in 1992 and 1993 and later on. Before the war, if you wanted to call a radio station in the former Yugoslavia, you had to put YU before the radio station's number. And all the ham radio operators from other states, when they heard "YU," they knew that the radio club was located somewhere in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. From the beginning of the war, the association of ham radio operators of Bosnia-Herzegovina decided that the call sign for Bosnia-Herzegovina would be 4N. The rest of the sign belonged to every particular radio club or radio station. It was the common practice by all the ham radio operators to introduce themselves during the first contact and say the entire code, irrespective of whether the contact was established within the state or with somebody outside of the state. In further communication, they avoided to say the sign for the state in order to be as brief as possible in their communication. It was a common practice, though, to use the entire code signal minus the two letters or numbers designating the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically if you look at this document, what's missing is the first two letters or two digits, 4N, which would be common to all ham operators over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Bosnia and Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the rest -- in other words, this is not as has been suggested someone who didn't know the call signal of Ilijas and tried to guess? This is someone who knew exactly that the call signal of Ilijas was 4N4SGS and left out the first two digits, 4N, as was the practice and still is the practice in many countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we've cleared that up as well. I'm sorry to intervene like this, but I think I need to intervene to keep --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because these are technical matters that we know very little about and anyone who is following knows probably less. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It helps us indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this report or both reports that you saw were drafted by the same author because the contents of the two are the same in any case. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence -- actually, I would like to tender both documents in evidence under one number, despite the fact that one already bears a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We don't have a problem with that. One last question before we do that. I don't know -- and I'm asking this question because I honestly cannot remember. Looking at the one document which ends with ERN number 7841, at the top right-hand corner, fourth handwritten line next to the date, to the right-hand side of the date, there seems to be a signature. Do you know whose signature is that? Can you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was my custom to put my shortened signature on the documents, and this resembles my shortened signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So this will be Defence Exhibit D265, no?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need a clip because I was playing with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question before the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, you told us that this resembles your signature, but you're not sure that this indeed is your signature. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be showing the witness two more documents, and I believe that this is a good time for a break because I am not able to do it within the three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, it's just a short procedural matter. We just filed before 4.00 a motion for protective measures and we have here a courtesy copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We already handed over the courtesy copy to the Defence and the Defence already expressed a positive response, a very positive response towards to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If that is the case, perhaps we can decide it here and now orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have considered the Prosecutor's motion, and our position is that we will not object to the protective measures due to the very specific job that the witness is engaged in and that mean that he might be exposed to some unpleasant situations. That's why we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber seized with a confidential motion -- let's go into private session, please. The witness, I think, needs to leave the courtroom for a while. It will only be one minute, the time to go out and come in again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the absence of the witness, just for the record --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- we have been able to provide the English version of document 01787841, and we have handed it over to Madam Registrar. That's the document that we have just discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For which the previous document forms part of it, okay? In the previous document Madam Vidovic said the two documents be put together and be given one number. This will form part of that document. Thank you. Yes. Your next question, Madam Vidovic. Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like the usher to provide the witness with the Prosecutor's document P307.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, the Prosecutor has shown you this document already. It is true, isn't it, that this document contains in the upper right corner the indication, communications officer. This is something that you yourself never used in communication?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. I have already said that in the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that you can't be sure that the rest of the document is credible, and I'm primarily referring to your signature. Are you in agreement with me when I say that you cannot be sure that the signature on the document is yours?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness another document, P79.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the document once you receive it. This is allegedly a document sent by the armed forces of Srebrenica. The number is 15/92, and the date is 19th September 1992. Mr. Becirovic, could you please look at the part after the word "subject," the title of the document. Do you agree with me it says here: "Draft decision regarding the setup of departments and appointing chiefs of these departments in the operations staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document therefore is a proposal to the War Presidency to issue a decision. Do you agree that this is exactly what the title of the document indicates?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has shown you this document and you have answered that during the year of 1999 [as interpreted] there was no communications department in the staff, and Muhamed Alic [as interpreted] did not work in the staff but in the centre for communications and information in the municipality of Srebrenica. In other words, this proposal regarding Hamed Alic has never taken off the ground. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer need this document. And now can the witness be shown another document. The number is 01787798.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please take a look at the document. This is a document issued by the War Presidency of municipality of Srebrenica. The number is 47/92, and the date is 16 August 1992. It was signed by Mr. Hajrudin Avdic on behalf of the War Presidency. It is a short document. I am going to read it to you. It says here order: The employees Evrim Vrankovina [phoen] and Sabahudin Gluhij to go to Suceska local commune on the 17th of August, 1992 in order to make a video recording of the war damage and general situation in the local commune of Suceska." In your testimony you have told us that the two persons who were recording were members of the service for communications and information, and that they were charged with recording of damaged factories and houses, and they were Sabahudin Gluhij and Evrim Vrankovina. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that together with them throughout the year 1992 and 1993, in addition to Nijaz Masic, there was also Mustafa Sacirovic who worked with them. Do you remember Mustafa Sacirovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him. He was --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he worked there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that he worked there. As far as I know, he did not start at the very beginning. He was there maybe in October and November, and in addition to them there was another person, a girl Elmedina Jamakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So all these people you have just referred to were gathering information for the War Presidency, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They would be given orders to make video recordings and to gather information on war crimes, and these orders were issued by the War Presidency. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move for this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document is being received and marked as document -- Defence Document D266.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have Madam Usher's assistance again. I would like to show the witness an OTP exhibit, and the number is P160. The document bears the following number: 01239547. The document purports to be a document of the armed forces of the subregion. The number is 194/92, and the date is 27 December 1992. The signature is communications and informations service of the subregion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, Mr. Becirovic, do you agree with me that you think that you sent this document based on your familiarity with the substance of this document and based on your belief that in the upper right corner we can find your signature. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the communications and information service of the subregion never existed in Srebrenica. There was no such thing there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you never put a stamp on any of the documents that you sent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, another question related to this document. Are you certain -- is there any way for you to be certain that the initial that this document bears belongs to you? Can you be positive about this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't be positive.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is no longer required. If I can have the usher's assistance, please, to show the witness yet another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the Srebrenica municipality subregion Bratunac/Vlasenica. The number is 118/9, the 18th of November, 1992. Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, subregion of Bratunac, Ministry of Defence, BH army, armed forces headquarters, and the public. I'm just quoting a portion of the document to save time. "Faced with the same problems and endangered by the same enemy, armed forces of Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and Zvornik gathered and put themselves under a single command, because these areas had been endangered by both Serbia and the extremist faction of the SDS for seven months already, and they have been completely surrounded. Recently the aggressor has piled up their armoured mechanised units along the Drina River and especially in Skelani and on the bridge on the Drina near Bratunac." Mr. Becirovic, let us leave aside for the time being the question whether this subregion, as a form of organisation, ever really got off the ground. There is something else that I want to ask you about this document. This document was sent to Sarajevo using a ham radio. Isn't that a fact? Is this something you can tell just by looking at the document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since November 1992 and onwards, you were in touch with Mr. Hamed Salihovic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He sent several reports like this to Sarajevo using your services in his capacity as the president of the War Presidency of the Srebrenica subregion. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were just several reports, not many though.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is safe to say that there was several such reports, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was never any other service that was sending these reports with the exception of the information service, of which you were an employee. There was no other subregional service of that kind. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. There was no other service like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His reports about the disastrous situation of the free areas of the Podravanje region were mostly produced in February and March of 1993. Would I be right in saying that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't be very specific about the time frame. The fact is, this was at least the way I remember, after the beginning of 1993, it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These were actually appeals launched to both the domestic public and the world, and he signed these in his capacity as president of the Presidency of the subregion. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that this document be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, Madam Vidovic, with its English -- corresponding English translation into English will be marked as Defence Exhibit 267 and 267E respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, along the same lines I have another question. It's true, isn't it, that Mr. Salihovic at some point early in November 1992 used your radio to send a report to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the general public, saying that he had been elected president of the subregion's War Presidency. Would I be right in stating that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now for something different. You testified that the ham radio communication lines were open and entirely unprotected in terms of confidential information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I said that a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have described listening in to the Serb forces using radios to talk about attacks. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you heard your enemy and their communications. You recorded this and passed it on to someone. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Any confidential reports sent in this way could always be intercepted by the enemy. That's a fair statement, isn't it, as long as they were radioed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Oric never used this line for military communications because you had pointed out to him the danger of being overheard or intercepted by the enemy. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite correct there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. At this point with respect to this question, I think it needs to be clear that Mr. -- if the question is that Naser Oric never used military communication, I think it should be with respect to -- in this witness's presence, I think if you go global, then this witness is just speculating at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's obviously as far as his being made available for such communication is concerned. He is not speaking -- You don't know whether actually Mr. Oric communicated with anyone else on military matters not involving you? You can't say that, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't possible for him to communicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We saw him yesterday -- or at least the Prosecution showed videos purporting to show him, you identified him as being Naser Oric, with a hand-held radio in his hands. What was he doing with it, playing with it? We also saw a dish antenna nearby. What was that for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did ID Naser Oric yesterday, and the device he was using is a short-range device. And in addition to seeing Naser Oric carrying this kind of equipment, I also saw Ibrahim Mandzic. He may have been somewhere nearby. Talking about the satellite dish, it was not part of the equipment that was ever used by Naser Oric. I suppose this was something used by the blue helmets or blue berets, if I can call them that. I can't tell you who these people were precisely. They may have been someone from UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, this is what my previous question was about. Oric was not using your line --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, Your Honours, I was talking about Mr. Becirovic's line specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- your line for military communication because you had pointed out to him the danger being intercepted by the enemy. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I believed it was my duty whenever anyone came to use my services and to use the radio that I should tell them that anything they said could easily be overheard or intercepted. Anything -- any traffic on the same frequency, including intercepted by the Serbs. I wanted to get people to talk about their families because that's what they were usually interested in. That's what they usually wanted, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Yesterday you identified Mr. Oric holding a type of radio device in his hand. You just told us that this was a short-range, low-power radio device. If you know, Mr. Becirovic, can you please specify the range of that device, or that type of device, if you like. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are low-power, low-range radios. If you have in mind the lie of the land in Srebrenica, the range could have been 10 kilometres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now to go back to the kind of communication that you were in charge of. Mr. Oric talked to Izetbegovic, Halilovic, and a person known as Munja who was from the 2nd Corps. The reason was that the pressure by the Serb forces during those talks had mounted to such an extent that it seemed very likely that Srebrenica would fall soon. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't identify Munja as someone who was necessarily in the 2nd Corps at the time. I was not aware of that. It was based on the gist of their conversation that I came to the conclusion that he may have been a member of the regional staff or of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, Witness. At the time these conversations occurred, I'm talking about the beginning of 1993 up to the run-up to the demilitarisation, so at this time Srebrenica was faced with the threat of genocide, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
