utterances.text: At the time the conversations took place, Mr. Oric was in fact quite conscious of the possibility that he was being intercepted, but there was no choice. He had no other way to come out and seek help for the people of Srebrenica. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would object that this is all speculation at this point. What -- I think the witness to testify to what his knowledge was of the ability, but outside of that I think that's pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it's one step short of speculation, Ms. Richardson. It stands to logic what the question was -- the way the question has been put is really asking the witness to confirm that it was logical for Mr. Oric to suspect or feel sure that any conversation would be intercepted. And the obvious answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my objection is to the line which went into whether or not Naser Oric had a choice, and that's where my objection lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered that already. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You used to see Mr. Oric at the time because he would come to see you to get in touch with his family. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever you met him throughout the war, he wore a beard, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, you stated that Oric would come to Srebrenica every now and then. Do you know that he actually spent the best part of his time in Potocari. Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that Potocari was a part of the defence line that was highly sensitive because of being subjected on a daily basis to attacks from the Bratunac area and the Kravica area?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If we leave aside what happened in Srebrenica in 1995, we would be entitled to say that the most difficult period in Srebrenica was that between mid-January 1993 and the 1993 demilitarisation, and you personally witnessed all these events. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would shift this time frame slightly, and I would put the beginning at late November and early December 1992 and then all the way to the demilitarisation period. If ever there was hell on earth, it was Srebrenica at the time under consideration. People were starving in a quite literal sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this is because since November, as you suggest, or December 1992 the Srebrenica area was being subjected to enormous pressure by the Serb forces, including those from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now, please. I would like to show the witness the following document. This is Defence Exhibit D184. This is a document produced by the War Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality. The number is 168/93, and the date is the 17th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look. I will quote a portion of this document. "Since the 1st of January this year" --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for your reference, Your Honours, this is the second passage of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that applies to you, Witness. It says: "The artillery attacks have been intensified since January 1st this year, and the former Yugoslav army air forces have been carrying out bombardments of the Srebrenica area every day and aircraft have been taking off from the Ponikve airport near Uzice. The world knows precious little about this. In night between the 15th and the 16th of January, 1993, the Uzice Corps crossed the bridge in Skelani from Bajina Basta with 12 tanks, seven APCs, and several trucks in order to carry out an attack against the territory held by the defenders. There has been heavy fighting since that moment and this fighting goes on as we speak. In the above-mentioned combat, the aggressor has been using the air forces and the result is that over 100 civilians have been killed. The aggressor's advance has been halted, but fresh forces are now being brought over from Serbia and sent into combat." Mr. Becirovic, do you agree that this document by the War Presidency faithfully reflects the situation throughout the Srebrenica area at the time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it was even worse than this, if anything. I see no reference here to the spreading diseases.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Becirovic. From the period described in this document to midway through 1993, there was the so-called winter offensive that was launched by the Serb forces. Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were attacks on Srebrenica and the surrounding villages that had remained free up to that point throughout February and March 1993. These attacks came from everywhere, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The pressure was enormous. One by one, the Muslim villages fell.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yet again, people were killed and the Muslims were expelled from the area?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There ensued a great amount of panic among the Muslims of Srebrenica and those who were in the villages around Srebrenica that were still free. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, when I say that throughout this period, January, February, and March 1993, Oric hardly ever, if at all, came to Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was where the going was really tough at the time. That's where he was. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now for something different. You knew Hazim Omerovic, didn't you, his nickname was Mrki. Did you know this person, Hazim Omerovic, also known as Mrki?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember really. There were several people who were called that. If you can specify, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hazim Omerovic, Mrki. Do you remember if Hazim Omerovic, Mrki, was someone who looked very much like Naser Oric? Was there another such person in Srebrenica, I mean Hazim Omerovic from Voljevica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a look-alike, and the person's name was Hazim. I'm not sure about the person's last name, but it might as well have been Omerovic. The nickname was Mrki.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: People who didn't know them very well would not have found it very difficult to confuse them, to mix them up?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would have been quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You heard, didn't you, that Hazim played all sorts of practical jokes about this and that he was in the habit of falsely identifying himself as Naser Oric. This is something that was going on in Srebrenica at the time. Did you hear anything about this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you give us some instances, for example, Mr. Becirovic, some instances of these practical jokes played by this Mrki?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been a long time since. I'm not sure I can remember. But he would very often accost girls and introduce himself as Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hazim Omerovic, also known as Mrki, was close to Akif Ustic, wasn't he? They were close. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They spent a lot of time together and this person spent a lot of time in Srebrenica itself, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had been expelled from Voljevica. He used to spend a lot of time with Akif Ustic, and he was a member of his group.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to radio communication. Radio communication involved a serious problem, and that was how to supply electric power to operate the radio. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Until November 1992, there had been a single generator that was used for the purposes of the hospital, and this generator was used to provide power to everyone else, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was as late as November 1992 at the Krizevici River that another electric engine was improvised, a makeshift one, that produced about 300 kilowatts of electrical energy and it was not a stable source of electricity, was it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is something I've already explained in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Until as late as the arrival of UNPROFOR and when UNPROFOR allowed you to use their sources of electricity, this remained the only source. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the package radio communication only took off in early March 1993. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This package line was used by a variety of people, including the War Presidency and all the other authorities, or is this perhaps something that you don't know about because that wasn't where you worked?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that it was used by the War Presidency and other authorities in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now, please, to show the witness the following document. This is a document issued by the ministry of the secretariat for national defence of the municipality of Bratunac. The date is 11 July 1994. It was signed by the secretary of the municipal secretariat for defence, and the computer number is 01838911. It was signed by Mr. Sadik Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at this document. We are not interested in the contents of the document, Mr. Becirovic. Just look at the left lower corner of this document. It says here, and I quote: "Agrees with the package, chairman of the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality, Fahrudin Salihovic." Is it true that Mr. Fahrudin Salihovic was the president of the War Presidency at the time in question?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, then it would be absolutely wrong to say that Mr. Oric controlled the package communication?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be 268. One question, Mr. Becirovic. Would it make you comment further if I pointed out that this document refers to what seems to Bratunac municipality and not to Srebrenica as such? This is -- submits such report for Bratunac municipality on personnel, livestock, structure and everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right there. As far as I know, in 1994 after the demilitarisation or long after it, the population of Bratunac who had been expelled to Srebrenica tried to establish their bodies of power in the villages of Cizmici and Bljecava, which belonged to the municipality of Bratunac. I believe that the reason for that -- that it is for that reason that they sent this document to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, whoever sent this document, Mr. Becirovic, had to have the agreement of the president of the War Presidency of Srebrenica, and this was done?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you have told us that before the war 17 local communes, or some of them which did not have telephone lines, before the war that is, had Iskra radio stations. Did I understand you well? You were talking about the prewar period, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know the lot of these prewar radio stations of the Iskra type, save for those you mentioned explicitly in your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The system of radio communication between the villages in Srebrenica municipality in the course of 1992 and early 1993 was never set up. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have testified about having made operational a ham radio station. You did not make operational any military radio equipment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is before the second half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, no military radio equipment or any such equipment existed in Srebrenica before the second half of 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I really do hate to interrupt, but perhaps if we could have clarification of what military radio equipment is being referred to. There are a number of different communications systems that this witness testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. You're 100 per cent right. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war you operated communication equipment, and you can make a difference between the military communication equipment and ordinary ham radio stations. Am I right in claiming that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that the former JNA had special military radio equipment and military radio stations?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing like that existed in Srebrenica before the second half of 1993. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also told us in the course of your testimony that you had contacts with many ham radio operators, sometimes even with those who were located in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, I had such contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within that context, are you familiar with the name Milos Okanovic? Does that name ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't ring any bells at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back to some other forms of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness Prosecutor's document number P7. This document bears the ERN number 01239517, which purposes to be the document of the armed forces of Srebrenica. The number is 51/92, and the date is 31 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a careful look at this document. I will read the relevant part to you. "Pursuant to the legally binding decree on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina (Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina 4/92) I hereby order all units of the armed forces of Srebrenica are to be assigned with the following codes: Armed forces staff, Suceska Brigade, Potocari Brigade, Kragljivoda Independent Battalion, and Srebrenica," and so on and so forth. Next to each of these names there is a number. Let me ask you this: It is true, isn't it, that on the 31st of October, or around that time, there were no brigades in the territory of Sebesic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was no mortar unit. Srebrenica did not have a mortar unit or platoon. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was no armoured company. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was not an engineering platoon either?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. There wasn't anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was no communications platoon on the 31st of October, 1992, or around that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was none.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the numbers next to the names in this document. You never saw these codes or numbers being used in the communication between any of the units. You actually never heard of units bearing certain number codes before the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And something else with regard to this document. The heading of this document of the introduction into it makes a reference to the decree law on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it mentions the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina 4/92. Mr. Becirovic, before the 31st of October, 1992, you never received any Official Gazette or a decree law either from Tuzla or from Sarajevo by means of the communication equipment that were at the disposal of your service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We haven't received any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A courier service between Srebrenica and other Muslim villages or Srebrenica and Tuzla was exceptionally dangerous. Did you hear that many people were killed in the attempt to transmit a message in that way?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, because correct me if I'm wrong but I am under the impression that yesterday when he was being asked about courier service for military communications he said that he's not aware that there was any. I stand to be corrected, but that's -- that's what I think he said yesterday. So if there were no couriers or courier service, how can he answer your question that many people died in trying to deliver messages? I don't know. It's up to you. I'm not going to ask any question myself, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the gist of my question was as follows: Did many men get killed in the attempt to act as couriers? That was the gist of my question. I'm not claiming that there were couriers, but that many men got killed in the attempt to carry messages. I don't know how this was recorded. In any case, I'm going to clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear, and I'm not claiming that there were courier services, but -- actually, I'm going to try to prove the contrary with the help of some documents. My question is: Did you hear that certain people did try to carry messages and that they got killed in that attempt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already answered that question in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. And now I would ask the usher to show the witness an excerpt from P84. The page bearing the follow number: 02115085. This is page 32 in the English version of this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, it is -- this is about a meeting of the armed forces which was held on the 4th of December, 1992. Would you please take a look at the first sentence on this page. This sentence reads: "Zulfo is saying, It is our big shortcoming that we go into action without any means of communication." Were you able to read that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without your help, I wouldn't be able to read this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is rather illegible, I agree. Once again, it is a big mistake to launch any actions without communication means. Then Smajo, then Ahmo says, and I quote: "Do you see here a paragraph where Ahmo is saying -- do you see the name Ahmo and I will quote. He says: "Our biggest shortcoming is communications. However, large sets of RUPs, mobile radio communications stations with batteries cannot be carried around." In connection with this, Mr. Becirovic, let me ask you this: This document reflects the real situation of communication between the units in the course of 1992 as late as December 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony so far I have tried to explain and I have stated that to my knowledge there were no communication means used by something that I didn't call the staff of the armed forces. I referred to those as poorly organised groups of people in the territory of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Let me ask you something else. This document confirms, doesn't it, that these people would go into action without any communication means?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you something else now about the RUP stations. When it comes to RUP stations, in order for them to be operational they had to have batteries?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The RUP set had to contain a battery for their power supply.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And for that you had to have electricity to charge those batteries?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Muslim villages around Srebrenica in the course of 1992 up to the demilitarisation in 1993, there was no electricity at all. Witness, leave aside Srebrenica. I'm asking you about the villages around Srebrenica. They did not have electricity. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. You're right. And I would say even after the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. occupation of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that you said "after the occupation of Srebrenica." Are you referring to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said until after the occupation of Srebrenica, until the moment people started coming back in 1997, 1998, and 1999. All of these villages had been burned down, and there was no electricity in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. You don't know whether it was possible at all for the batteries to be charged, for the RUP stations to be operational if there were any, or do you perhaps think that this was not at all possible?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not at all possible to charge those batteries if they existed. I'm not aware of the existence of RUP stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you have also told us that the RUP frequency was not enough to reach Suceska from Srebrenica due to the lay of the hilly terrain. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is also true that the entire area of Srebrenica and the surrounding villages is rather hilly?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The RUP communication in such areas, even if the RUP stations could have been operational, would have been practically impossible. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are, and this is for two reasons. First of all is the source of energy and the second is the layout of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the RUP station in Srebrenica was made operational only after the end of 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The attempt for the villages to become connected started in August 1993, that is after the demilitarisation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The -- when we're talking about communication suing a RUP, if this communication had been possible, it would have been open and exposed to the interception by the enemy. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, the Prosecutor asked you about the Atlas radio. The question was whether it was possible to communicate between Srebrenica and Cerska using this type of radio. Let me put it this way: Many things are possible, Mr. Becirovic, however you are not aware of the fact that somebody from Srebrenica used an Atlas radio in order to communicate with Cerska and vice versa. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony I said that in December 1992 an Atlas radio station 210X was mounted in Cerska. The intention was to try and send the information to Tuzla and Sarajevo about the situation in that area. Because of the layout of the ground, communication with Sarajevo was not possible. On several occasions, I communicated with that radio station in Cerska from Srebrenica. The reception was very bad, but the fact is that during that brief period of time while that Atlas radio existed in Cerska before Cerska fell, we could establish several contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Oric did not communicate with Cerska in this way?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Oric did not communicate with this way. I also said that the information that I received from Cerska I forwarded to the general public. I would summarise the information and I would join it with the information that I myself collected in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, again we are talking about your appeals and reports on the very difficult situation that prevailed in Cerska that was faced with a major disaster?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now for something different. Mr. Becirovic, you know, don't you, that in Tuzla there was a group of people from the Srebrenica area, people who had left the Srebrenica area at the beginning of the war. These people established a body whose name was also the Srebrenica Territorial Defence Staff. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that this body was in touch with the district defence staff and the authorities in Tuzla. Do you have any information on that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on information that I obtained later, it was in the second half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If this body in Tuzla that called itself the Srebrenica Territorial Defence Staff received any documents in May, June, and July 1992 and later, this would not mean that these documents were really received by the Territorial Defence Staff in Srebrenica, would it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1992 you never received anything through this Territorial Defence Staff that was based in Tuzla via communications equipment, you received nothing from the district defence staff in Tuzla or any other bodies based in Tuzla, did you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier I testified that communication was only one way, from Srebrenica out and not back into Srebrenica. Nothing from Sarajevo or Tuzla ever reached Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now. I would like to show the witness a document. This is an OTP document. The number is P29. This is P29. It's a document by the district defence staff -- Territorial Defence Staff is Tuzla. The number is 01/31. The date is 28th of May, 1992. The ERN number is 01819864.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please go through this document in its entirety and please pay close attention. The title of this document is Acts and Behaviour of the Members of the Territorial Defence Unit in relation to the population during combat activities. This is an order signed by commander Lieutenant Colonel Zeljko Knez. This document is an order to stop the burnings, the lootings of both mobile and immobile property of the population during and after combat by TO units in the areas where there were combat activities. Please, Witness, if you could have a look at this document. Once you've looked at that, can you please look at the left corner. It says, delivered to the Tuzla municipal staff, Zivinice, Lukavac, abbreviation, Kalesija, Srebrenica, Gradacac, Banovici and files. First of all, Witness, you have never seen this document before, have you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In late May 1992, the communications and information service of which you were on employee had not even been set up, had it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hamed Alic set up a communications line to the outside world in late June 1992, and he used a fax machine. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document closely now. This was not something that was faxed to Srebrenica and received by fax in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such document having been received.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the document itself. There is nothing to suggest, unlike some of the previous documents, that this document was received by fax?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the information service did not receive this document in Srebrenica, not in any way in fact. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just saying this calls for speculation. We've gone through the fax machine. Now the witness is being asked if this has ever been received in Srebrenica. As far as he knows, through the mechanism he's aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague has just drawn my attention to something. There was no way I said what the transcript reflects. I asked the witness the following question: This document never came to Srebrenica through the communications and information service that you worked for? I was very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't that my question, Witness? Wasn't that your understanding of my question?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That solves the problem. Let's proceed to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the end of May and the beginning of June 1992 was a period of heavy fighting in the area between Srebrenica and Tuzla. Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this would be a very convenient time to break. I don't have many questions left, but this would be a very good time. I have a bit of a sore throat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that will leave time for re-examination if there is going to be one and also some time for us to put some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. How much more do you think you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 15 or 20 minutes tops, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to use no more than 15 minutes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It makes it difficult. So I'm going to impose an embargo now. 15 minutes for you, Madam Vidovic; 10 minutes for you; and the rest for us. Thank you. And let's have a shorter break, 20 minutes instead of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's try to finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be very brief but I do feel a need to say something. The Defence, especially myself, are someone who really appreciates the Tribunal and we're trying to do our best to help. But one thing I'm very unhappy about is that the Prosecutor every time oversteps the mark and the allotted time, the time allotted by the Trial Chamber, which puts me in a spot, and I always have to keep my cross-examination as brief as I possibly can. I understand that, and out of respect to the Trial Chamber I will oblige. I understand that you need to ask certain questions, too. But in relation to our future witnesses, especially these three or four, we find them at least as important as the OTP. So if both parties are allotted a certain time limit, I think we should both do our best to comply with the time limit. We will certainly try to do our best. I've never had any complaints with regard to this, but I would just like to say that we certainly should expect the OTP to stick to their allotted time, just like we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in actual fact, you've both exceeded the time that you had indicated in the first place, and of course I can understand that happening in the Defence much more than I can understand it happening from the Prosecution's side. But it won't happen again; we told you this very clearly yesterday. From now onwards you will each have a time limit and we will not allow one single minute beyond that. In the meantime, we have lost another minute. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance now, please. If I can please show the witness the following document 02622758, P143. P143.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the Tuzla district staff. The date is the 14th of October, 1992. This is an order signed by Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, go straight to the question. You don't need to tell the witness what there is or us what there is on this document; we can see it. Your question, go straight to the question and you will finish all the questions that you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Witness, can you look at the upper part of this document, the top half. In the upper right-hand corner you can see first the incoming stamp of the Kladanj 3 operations group and then the incoming stamp of the Municipal Assembly of Kladanj and the Kladanj Territorial Defence Staff. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document was received in Kladanj, which is quite a long way from Srebrenica. Can you please tell us the distance between the two, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please go through the entire document closely. There is nothing in this document that appears to indicate that the document was ever received in Srebrenica, does it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first sight, there is nothing to indicate that the document was ever received in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is no incoming stamp of any kind, no signature, nothing at all to indicate that the document was ever received in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is no longer required. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you some questions now about a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now show the witness P208. This purports to be a document by the armed forces staff in Srebrenica 3/93. The date is the 4th of January, 1992. I will quote the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, you saw this document yesterday. I am now quoting. It says: "Order on readiness. Deliver. Do nothing without an agreement with Naser first. Be at the ready if Naser needs you and await further orders. The radio is to be put into operation immediately and respond regularly. This order was received by radio." Mr. Becirovic, this document was purportedly written by your brother. You knew your brother well, didn't you? You were familiar with the way he wrote and spoke, were you not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your brother was an educated man and he knew how to write, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was known as a pedantic person, a neat person, a well-organised around Srebrenica, was he not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that this document was written in an extremely incoherent manner, and this seems to suggest an author who was not well-educated and not particularly given to writing documents?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your brother would never have written or signed anything like this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this calls for speculation at this point. We're talking about an order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Rephrase your question, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your brother, therefore, would never produce a document that did not reflect a certain education background. Anything he produced would have seemed like the product of an educated person, which might lead you to believe that this document was not produced by your brother. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right in saying that this was definitely not my brother, Ramiz's, style.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really do hate to object. I know we're short on time. But I think that with respect to what was produced by this witness's brother, via what he knows about the brother, I think that there should have been some foundational questions put to this witness about whether he has ever seen any order written by his brother, does this conform in fact to similar documents he's seen. And I think any answer that he has given at this point, even though he has given one, is speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, Madam Vidovic. I'm not going to tell Madam Vidovic what questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, do you have any suspicions whether your brother actually produced this document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have my suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified that Naser had the nickname Gazda and that this nickname was used in his conversation with a person known as Munja. Do you agree with me when I say that the nickname Gazda is a very frequent nickname where we come from? Would that not be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Many people when talking address each other using such words as Gazda, boss, chef, also meaning boss. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was perfectly normal for local commanders to introduce themselves as Gazda or for other people to address them using this word. Is this something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was normal practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Many people in prominent positions would be addressed as Gazda or would in fact introduce themselves as Gazda, not just commanders, other prominent people, too. This is something that is usual where we come from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case both before the war and throughout the war. This was a perfectly normal thing for people who were in any way prominent, perhaps well-off or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't really say that Naser was the only person in the area who used this sobriquet name Gazda or who were referred to as Gazda, could you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have also time for objections, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, you were shown documents -- a document by the Defence, and that is document 267.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what time did Ms. Richardson start?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 267.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this -- without giving you the document again for you to review in the interests of time, this document you testified indicated that Hamed Salilovic had sent a message as -- within the position that he held as the War Presidency of the subregion. I believe you agreed with the Defence that this document had been sent. Secondly, when you were asked how this document was sent you said it was sent via ham radio. Now, on this document itself there's an indication that it was received by Ilijas Omerovic and it was sent to Sarajevo. Now, I will read for you the numbers for the ham radio, the amateur radio station that received this document, and that is 4N4SGS. Now, having heard those numbers and letters, does this reflect that this document in fact went to that station, based on your knowledge of the station and the numbers that were used?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my communication with Ilijas Omerovic, I could recognise his modulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So indeed, if other documents which I believe the Defence indicated one -- one such document where it was sent to Ilijas and only 4SGS was used, that would not be an indication that it was not sent to him. Is that correct? Because here -- let me finish my question -- here's an indication that all of the numbers were used, and it was never -- and your testimony was that it was sent to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the witness -- witness should have the document before him if asked to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not waste time on this very much because in the Trial Chamber's mind it's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for Malta an amateur radio -- ham radio operator, apart from requiring a license, will always have a 9H, and that is the indicative of Malta, and then he explained what the rest is. When you are communicating, they have a system of cards that they keep and that the modulation that they send and receive, and you know this is all oral, verbal. I mean, this is not something sent -- you're not transmitting a document in the sense that a paper goes in and comes out of the other end. This is all a verbal conversation, an oral conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I'm just seeking to make sure there is no misunderstanding with respect to the consistency of the receiver and the radio station, which is why I would like the witness to just briefly look at the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, if you can, in the document before you, it's indicated in the lower left-hand corner, it's the very last piece of information that's indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question basically is this, Mr. Becirovic, in case it's not clear in your mind. The fact that on the document that you are seeing you don't have the entire call sign, you don't have the initial 4N, would that put any doubt in your mind that that transmission or that -- that transmission could have never taken place? Or is it a way you record -- you and other colleagues of yours record things just to speed up the procedure? Because anyone you are communicating with in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia would always have 4N? Or in Bosnia would always have 4N, so you don't need to write that. All you need to write are the remaining four characters for the purposes of your record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document I have only the signal of the radio club in Sarajevo, and the 4SGS received information, the information that I sent. And this sign confirms that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you don't need to have 4N to confirm that that message has been sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that that was clear, Your Honour. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Becirovic, with respect to Prosecution Exhibit 29E that was shown to you, and I've just referred to the document. It was in reference to a document issued by Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Zeljko Knez. And this -- it was asked if you recall receiving this document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, my question to you is whether or not you were present on the 20th of May [sic] at the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica. Do you recall if on that day you were present or the day after you had a meeting with them or was present?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not present during this particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And so that we're clear you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now wait one moment. Now, yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had an objection. The witness never said that he was present at the meeting of the Territorial Defence Staff on the 20th. The question was: Do you remember that you were present on that day? Did you have a meeting with them? The witness never said anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is -- my question to you is whether or not you were present on the 20th of May at the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica? Do you recall if on that day you were present or on the day after you had a meeting with them or was present? There is no allegation at any time that he was. He's being asked whether he was present or not, whether he recalls any such presence. I mean, it's not being suggested to him that he was. Anyway, let's move, because we are running short of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And my question to you is: You don't know if this document had been delivered by hand or courier or by any other means, do you, to the Srebrenica armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object again. The document was issued on the 28th of May. The Prosecutor is now confusing the witness, asking him about the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 28th of May, and I'm not sure if in the transcript, it says the 20th, but it is certainly the 28th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript showed 20th, 2-0.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I certainly need that corrected. It's the 28th. Not meant at all to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record wherever there is 20th in this part of the transcript, it should be 28 and not 20th. Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, you were also asked to review minutes which contained information about whether or not there was any communication ability within the armed forces of Srebrenica. And my question to you is whether or not you attended any War Presidency meetings or any meetings of the Srebrenica municipal forces during 1992 and 1993, specifically October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was never present at the sessions of the War Presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica or any other organisation for that matter. I've already said that I'm not aware of the fact that there was an organised Territorial Defence Staff of the municipality of Srebrenica, not before the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with respect to my last series of questions I asked about whether or not the witness was aware of whether the document had been delivered by hand or courier. I don't think the witness ever answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he answered as yet. That particular document that you were shown last, supposedly signed by Mr. Knez -- well, not signed but attributed to general or Commander Knez, are you -- can you tell us whether it was to your knowledge ever delivered to the -- you restricted it only to the territorial staff, didn't you, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To the territorial staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: By courier or hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By courier or by --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Or by any other means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any manner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Your Honour, this document never reached Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. With respect to my next question, it has to do with whether or not you attended any of the territorial staff meetings and I believe, if I'm not mistaken, that you said that you did not. And so I would like to read for you from page 5 of P84. If you would listen I would read it very quickly. It's dated October 3rd, 1992. Present unit commanders under number 9 it says communication. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it on the -- we need to show it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: ERN number to the specific page is 02115047.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it is page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you can start --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Number 9. It states: "The military police must take mobile radio transmitters and walkie-talkies. They must be distributed. The command post is at the anti-aircraft machine-gun sight. The pass word is Bosna Dzihad, and it lists the number of troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, as far as you know, you were not involved in this meeting, were you, where these things were discussed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was not involved in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And I just have one more question with respect to the same document and that is ERN number 02115087 [sic] and this was the -- just a follow-up question with respect to what had been asked earlier. It is page, excuse me, 33 of the English version of the document. ERN number 02115085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 5085 you have to look at. Yes, your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My question is there's a portion after Zulfo Tusunovic it's a comment being made by Smajo or Samo [phoen]. It states, the second sentence: "The motors telephoned our attacks. A big mistake was made during reconnaissance. My group was last to retreat." Now -- and secondly I'll read what Ahmo said. "Our biggest shortcoming is communication. We have a large sets with batteries. Cannot be carried around." Now, in fact there is no indication here that this communication equipment was not operational at the time, is there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may give you my view of this period, in the course of my testimony I have already stated that there were no RUP equipment or any other means of communication that could be used in this way and that could be commented upon in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, if you could answer my question. In fact, this information here does not state that the equipment is not operational, does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, it just says that it is not practical to carry them around. It does not purport to state that they are not operational if they existed. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If it relates to the question, let him answer it first; if it relates to the transcript, then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the person says two sentences and the Prosecutor just reads one. These two sentences are related. The Prosecutor is confusing the witness in this way. The speaker uttered two sentences, not just one, and this is how it should be presented to the witness. In other words, it says: "Our biggest shortcoming are communications," and then this is followed by the sentence that the Prosecutor read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, this is the last time I'm saying this. I gave you instructions not to proceed if the objection that you had related to the answer that the question was supposed to -- that the witness was supposed to give. Don't do this again because I will take further steps. Now, the -- Ms. Richardson had read the first part as well and her question is a very simple one. Does that mean that -- does that part of the statement indicate that these RUP or whatever they are called were not operational or that that was just not practical to carry them around? That's the question that was asked. So answer it -- please answer -- give us your answer and let's please move to the next question. And this was my final warning. I will not tolerate interruptions before the witness has given the -- his answer. I mean, I will give the go ahead, and if I tell you to stop, stop. And I told you very clear, if you have got comments to make on the transcript, yes, go ahead. If it's relating to the question itself, stop. And if you don't, there will be -- there will be consequences. Yes. Witness, what does that actually say? Does it say that there were RUPs that were not operational, or that there were RUPs which couldn't, however, be carried -- carried around, was not practical to carry them around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the gist of this sentence is as follows: The RUPs were not practical to be carried around. But as I've already said earlier, I was not aware of the existence of the RUP equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. You can't be expected to know everything. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one last question and again it pertains to this document. If the usher could assist. It's page 17, the English version, the ERN is 02115064. The previous page is dated the 3rd of November, 1992, but the actual page that I'd like to make reference to is 02115064. And it states: "As for the work of communication and information service, in fact it consists of two services, the communications service operating within the armed forces and the information service, something is illegible, it is believed that a special commission of the War Presidency must be formed from the communication and information service for information regarding war destruction and losses." Now, Mr. Becirovic, you I believe already testified that you did not attend meetings of the armed forces. You are not familiar with this -- you weren't advised of this information, were you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the fact that there were two services for communication and information. I can't read this text, and if I understand your question well you're asking me whether there were two services for communication and information. And as I've already said, I'm not aware of that. I know that there was one service for communication and information, and it was part of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I guess my final question is: Since you did not attend the -- the meetings, you weren't advised of this particular information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't follow, Ms. Richardson, it doesn't follow necessarily. If there was a decision that it was believed that a special commission of the War Presidency must be formed from that, it would have been formed and he may have come to know about it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, I have now only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Could you give us the exact date when the telephone lines to Srebrenica was cut, or roughly the date?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know the exact date. This was sometime mid-July 1992 or maybe even in the first half of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I am still in need of clarification with regard to this reporting system, how you reported and how you collected your reports. You told us that you gathered your information that you sent out to Sarajevo and to the world by asking people who have been in the hospital, wounded people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, would the usher please put Defence Exhibit 265 on the ELMO. Now, in September -- in the September 1992, I think it was, if I remember correctly, it was that Hamed Alic still was in Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, if you look to this document, it reads: "Around 10.00, criminals from Podravanje military attacked the villages of Kutuzero, Derventa, Zutica, and Suceska," then it goes in a speedy and effective action the Srebrenica armed forces moved to counter attack on the line Suceska, Kutuzero, and Bucje villages. In exceptionally well-prepared sabotage actions, a Chetnik Bracan stronghold was taken. A T-53 tank and a PAT anti-aircraft gun were quickly seized from the aggressor and two armoured personnel carriers were destroyed." Now, I guess these are different villages that are mentioned here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, if you wanted to collect information from these villages, I suppose that you would have had wounded people in the hospital from all these villages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, this does not have to be so, but it is correct. The territory of Suceska local commune had about 25 to 30 hamlets in the area covering about 10 square kilometres. So a wounded who came from one village was also aware of the happenings in other villages. To be more specific, in this particular attack, the Serb forces launched a fierce attack from Milici and Podravanje. Those are the western and the southern axes of the local commune of Suceska. All the wounded who arrived in the Srebrenica hospital from any of the villages were able to know and could hear what happened in the other villages, in the villages that they themselves were not from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: They could also hear and observe what was seized by the army? Or by the fighters, let's put it this way, by the fighters.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I believe that I've already said that the credibility of this information depended on the accuracy of what people told me. I never checked how many people were captured, if any. So I can't say this information was received a day after the attack. And it was drafted on the 25th of September, a day after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, another question. You told us about the use of these communication devices in the PTT where other people, civilians, were able to use it to get in touch with their families. And in your testimony yesterday you told us that members of the Territorial Defence in cases where they tried to stay in touch with their families using this equipment, they had a chance of using the equipment under my control. Now, what do you mean with "under my control"? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that amongst others, members of the Territorial Defence used my services, which means that I was the one who was supposed to establish contact with a ham radio operator in another place. When that contact was established, I handed the mike over to the person who actually wanted to talk, and I was present during that conversation of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you could overhear everything that was spoken during this communication?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, you also told us that General Morillon was using this communication. Should I conclude from your answers that you would also overhear what General Morillon was talking with other people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I was able to hear what General Morillon was saying. But I do not speak French and French was the language he used. So at the end of the conversation, there would be an interpreter who would convey to me the gist of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Then you also testified with establishing a communication with a man called Munja and that he wanted to get in touch with Naser Oric. Now, how did you get in touch with Naser Oric? What was the way of telling him that he is wanted by Munja to talk -- have a talk with him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I've explained, people came over almost every day to get in touch with their families. I can't remember any specific details of notifying Naser, but the usual thing to do would be to use someone from the Potocari area to get the message to Naser. The message would say that there was a person called Munja who wanted to speak to Naser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, coming back -- my last question to today's testimony with regard to the presence of Naser Oric in the period of January, February, and March 1993 in Srebrenica, and you have been asked by the Defence: He was where the going was really tough at the time. That's where he was. Isn't that the case? And you would answer "yes." Now, what would have been these tough places that you assume that he was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fringe areas of the Srebrenica free territory. I mean the general Potocari area, the Suceska area, the Kragljivoda, and the Osata [phoen] area. If we imagine a circle there, the radius would amount to about 30 or 40 kilometres. It was a very small area at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Vidovic did not mention any places. Now, how can you suppose that she had the same places in mind which you described now?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When she said where the situation at its worst, what I took that to mean was places where there was the heaviest fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I don't have any questions for you, which brings us to the end of your testimony, Mr. Becirovic. I thank you on behalf of the Tribunal; on behalf of the Trial Chamber; on behalf of my colleague, Judge Brydensholt, from the Kingdom of Denmark; and Judge Eser from Germany; and also on my own behalf. I thank you for having come over to give testimony in this case, for also having stayed here more than I thought you were needed to stay, but I thank you. You will now receive all the assistance that you need from the staff of this Tribunal to facilitate your return back home at the earliest opportunity. I can assure you that that assistance will be forthcoming immediately the moment you walk out of this courtroom. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher. And my last words to you, also on behalf of everyone present here, is that we all wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, tomorrow we sit in the afternoon like today. We have agreed that the new witness will testify with special protective measures that we have agreed upon, thanks to the cooperation of the Defence. We need to decide for how long she is going to be. You said three hours, you need three hours, Ms. -- I don't know who is going to be responsible for that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, tomorrow that will be Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio. And what we would like to do from the Prosecution's stance is to -- instead of enunciating how many hours, three hours, five hours, is to speak in terms of the days needed to testify. And I have been informed that this witness will take no longer than tomorrow and that there's a possibility that the direct examination will be shorter than one full court day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That -- so the position is as follows -- how much time do you require, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm answering because I'll be cross-examining the witness. I wanted to put it really this way: That looking at the potential testimony to be given by this witness, if the Prosecution adopt a fairly sensible approach and limit the testimony to really what that witness can testify about, which is actually in our submission fairly limited, in other words, if Mr. Di Fazio adopts a sensible approach and he's a pretty sensible chap, then I think I can be finished fairly quickly, within an hour or an hour and a half. I think, you know -- if we do adopt a sensible approach with this witness, perhaps the witness can be completely finished within one day, cross-examination and re-examination. So I could certainly be very brief with this witness, provided the witness stays within what that witness can reasonably testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. When is the next witness arriving in The Hague, number 44?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness should be arriving this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is in charge of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'll be taking that witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So start proofing him as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As of 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So that if we can advance his testimony to before the 2nd of May, we'll try to do that. This is going to be a crucial witness, as I see it, and the sooner we start, the better.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We anticipate starting him and we will try and do it as soon as possible. I think the Prosecution also would like to inform you that there is a possibility that if witness protection is required we will file a written motion on that also as soon as possible for deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, if you file that, I think it can be decided tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But what I mean to say is this: If there is a slight possibility that we would finish with this next witness tomorrow, then let's not waste the next day. So this is why I'm saying try to get the proofing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- cracking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If we did finish with this next witness tomorrow, using all sense and sensibilities on behalf of both parties, I do think that it would be highly impossible to start with that next witness the day afterwards anyway. This witness has been allowed to have an appropriate time period for proofing. We've had to, as a matter of fact, ask for special measures. I believe that the Defence certainly would be sensibly in agreement with us to not limit our proofing to one day on this witness. And I do believe that only in proofing him could we reach absolutely the core of what the Trial Chamber would want to hear without going into other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. -- you must have misunderstood me. I never meant to say that your examination-in-chief will be limited to one day or that the proofing will be limited to one day. I'm just saying that if you can, get the proofing process cracking and make it possible to start with this witness on the 28th instead the 2nd -- of the 2nd May. If that is at all possible, then please do it, because it seems to me that there is a great possibility of finishing with tomorrow's witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that it will take longer than one day to proof this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To proof this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And we will not be able to start on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll deal with this tomorrow. Good evening everybody, and we'll meet again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of April, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
